hook: Why do averages of many random outcomes settle down, and how large are the fluctuations that remain?
about: Probability theory is the mathematics of chance. It assigns numbers between 0 and 1 to events and works out the consequences, from coin tossing to the motion of a pollen grain in water. Stochastic processes, which are random quantities that evolve in time, form a large part of the area. Examples are random walks, Markov chains and Brownian motion.

Since the 1930s the subject has been built on measure theory, with probabilities treated as measures and random variables as measurable functions. A recurring theme is that large random systems show regular behavior: averages converge and fluctuations follow universal laws. Probability supplies the language for statistics, statistical physics and mathematical finance, and probabilistic arguments are used in analysis, combinatorics and number theory.

example.title: Shared birthdays
example.text: Put 23 people in a room and assume birthdays are independent and uniform over 365 days. The chance that all 23 birthdays differ is \(\frac{365}{365}\cdot\frac{364}{365}\cdots\frac{343}{365} \approx 0.493\). So the chance that at least two people share a birthday is about \(0.507\), a little more than one half. With 50 people it rises to about \(0.97\).

objects.gloss: A set of outcomes, a collection of events and a measure assigning each event a probability.
A measurable function that assigns a number to each outcome.
The probability-weighted average of a random variable.
Events or variables are independent when the probability of joint occurrences is the product of individual probabilities.
A random process whose next step depends only on its current state.
A continuous random path with independent, normally distributed increments.
A process whose expected future value, given the past, equals its present value.

theorems.name: Strong law of large numbers
theorems.statement: If \(X_1, X_2, \dots\) are independent and identically distributed with \(E|X_1| < \infty\) and mean \(\mu\), then \((X_1 + \cdots + X_n)/n \to \mu\) almost surely.

theorems.name: Central limit theorem
theorems.statement: If \(X_1, X_2, \dots\) are independent and identically distributed with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(0 < \sigma^2 < \infty\), then \((X_1 + \cdots + X_n - n\mu)/(\sigma\sqrt{n})\) converges in distribution to the standard normal law.

theorems.name: Convergence theorem for Markov chains
theorems.statement: An irreducible aperiodic Markov chain on a finite state space has a unique stationary distribution \(\pi\), and from every starting state the distribution of the chain at time \(n\) converges to \(\pi\) as \(n \to \infty\).

theorems.name: Martingale convergence theorem
theorems.statement: A martingale \((M_n)\) with \(\sup_n E|M_n| < \infty\) converges almost surely to a limit with finite expectation.

theorems.name: Itô's formula
theorems.statement: If \(B\) is a standard Brownian motion and \(f\) is twice continuously differentiable, then almost surely \(f(B_t) = f(B_0) + \int_0^t f'(B_s)\,dB_s + \frac12\int_0^t f''(B_s)\,ds\) for all \(t \ge 0\).

theorems.name: Donsker's invariance principle
theorems.statement: Let \(S_n\) be a random walk whose steps are independent and identically distributed with mean 0 and variance 1. The rescaled, linearly interpolated paths \(t \mapsto S_{nt}/\sqrt{n}\) on \([0,1]\) converge in distribution, as random continuous functions, to Brownian motion.

open.name: Self-avoiding walk in the plane
open.gloss: Show that a uniformly random \(n\)-step self-avoiding walk on a planar lattice typically travels a distance of order \(n^{3/4}\).

open.name: Critical percolation in three dimensions
open.gloss: Prove that there is no infinite open cluster at the critical probability on the cubic lattice.

open.name: KPZ universality
open.gloss: Show that a wide class of random growth models share the fluctuation exponents and limit laws found in a few exactly solvable cases.
